title: This time is different? Speech by Sarah Breeden
summary: Bank of England Deputy Governor for Financial Stability Sarah Breeden delivered a speech examining the current financial stability landscape, noting that while post-GFC reforms have built proven resilience in banking, risks have migrated to market-based finance (now ~50% of UK/global financial sector assets), sovereign balance sheets, and private markets. She highlighted three key vulnerabilities: private markets (grown to ~$18 trillion globally), elevated sovereign debt near post-war highs, and complex interconnections in the financial ecosystem that could amplify shocks.
key_points: Global financial system has absorbed six major shocks in six years (pandemic, Russia-Ukraine war, overseas bank failures including a G-SIB, UK gilt market stress in 2022, trade disruptions, energy shock) without amplifying them
Banking sector resilience is confirmed: banks hold significantly more and higher-quality capital and liquidity; UK bank stress tests show ability to continue lending through severe scenarios
Household indebtedness is close to its lowest level since early 2000s, with low arrears and manageable debt-servicing burdens; corporate balance sheets also appear more resilient
Activity has migrated from banks to market-based finance, which now accounts for around half of UK and global financial-sector assets

Private market assets under management have grown ~6x since 2008/9 to roughly $18 trillion by 2025; BoE highlights vulnerabilities in transparency, lagging valuations, weakened underwriting standards, and complex leverage layers

Sovereign debt in advanced economies is now close to post-war highs, reducing fiscal space and increasing sensitivity to shifts in market confidence; UK gilt market stress in autumn 2022 is cited as example of sovereign bond market plumbing risk
why_it_matters: This speech is significant for understanding how financial system vulnerabilities have evolved since the GFC. The shift from bank-based to market-based finance means risks have migrated to less regulated, less transparent segments. The $18 trillion private markets sector has not been stress-tested at scale by a broad-based macroeconomic shock in a higher-rate environment. Sovereign debt at post-war highs reduces governments' ability to absorb future shocks. These structural shifts have implications for systemic risk monitoring, regulatory priorities, and market participants assessing where stress could crystallize.
macro_context: While primarily a market structure speech, it provides macro context: sovereign bond markets anchor pricing for mortgages and corporate credit and provide core collateral for repo and derivatives markets. Sharp rises in government bond yields tighten financing conditions across the economy. The BoE sees the shift of risk to sovereign balance sheets as a key vulnerability that reduces fiscal space to respond to future shocks.
market_structure_context: Sovereign bond markets provide core collateral for repo and derivatives markets—the plumbing of the financial system. When that plumbing fails, stress propagates quickly, as seen in UK autumn 2022. Private markets have grown to $18 trillion with complex leverage layer-caking at borrower, fund, and sponsor level. Loans are sliced into CLOs and distributed based on ratings agency assessments. Complex connections to banks, insurers, and reinsurers create an ecosystem where losses become hard to trace.

6 (number of major shocks absorbed by financial system in 6 years)
